title: One-way electron mirrors from single-layer stacking shifts in rhombohedral graphite
authors: Konrád Kandrai, András Balogh, Dóra Varga, Márton Szendrő, András Pálinkás, József Cserti, János Koltai, Krisztián Márity, Péter Vancsó, Géza I. Márk, Alexandre Mayer, Zoltán Tajkov, Levente Tapasztó, Péter Nemes-Incze
abstract: One-way mirrors or asymmetric scatterers are key components of photonic systems, protecting sources from back-reflections and routing light along a chosen path. Acoustic systems can also be engineered to show asymmetric reflection. However, a condensed matter platform acting as a one-way mirror without breaking linearity, time-reversal symmetry or energy conservation has been lacking. One route to achieving this is mode selection, where a probe coupled to only some modes sees a boundary as a mirror from one side and as transparent from the other. Here we show that single-layer stacking shifts in six-layer rhombohedral graphite provide this platform, acting as one-way mirrors for electrons. In scanning tunneling microscopy, 10 nm scale interference fringes appear only on the stacking fault side of a wall, tracking its Dirac band, the rhombohedral side remaining transparent. Layer-resolved tight-binding and wave-packet dynamics calculations reproduce this and trace the asymmetry to the mismatched layer polarization across the wall, with the tip supplying the selective coupling. Because stacking solitons glide under external fields, this mirror forms a movable element of electron optics defined by the crystal structure alone.
summary: This work demonstrates that stacking faults in rhombohedral graphite can function as one-way electron mirrors for electrons. By combining STM measurements with detailed electronic structure calculations, the authors attribute this directional asymmetry to mode selection at the domain wall. This establishes a novel, structure-defined building block for electron optics in condensed matter systems.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of creating a condensed matter platform that functions as a one-way electron mirror without violating fundamental symmetries like linearity or time-reversal symmetry.
main_result: Single-layer stacking shifts in rhombohedral graphite successfully act as one-way electron mirrors, demonstrated by observing interference fringes only on the stacking fault side of the boundary.
method: The study combines Scanning Tunneling Microscopy (STM) measurements (QPI) with advanced theoretical calculations, including layer-resolved tight-binding and wave-packet dynamics.
model_or_system: The physical system is six-layer rhombohedral graphite containing stacking faults, which are modeled using electronic structure calculations and analyzed via STM measurements.
key_observables: Appearance and tracking of 10 nm scale interference fringes in the Local Density of States (LDOS), and the asymmetry in electron scattering across the domain wall.
important_parameters: The asymmetry is attributed to mode selection, which is controlled by the selective coupling provided by the STM tip.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the asymmetry arises from mode selection due to the mismatched layer polarization across the stacking fault, rather than a symmetry-breaking potential.
figures_summary: Figures show schematic atomic structures of the graphite domains, STM dI/dV maps revealing standing waves in the LDOS on the fault side, and plots analyzing the energy dependence of these interference fringes.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the need for a symmetric one-way mirror, presents STM evidence of asymmetric scattering in graphite stacking faults, and then uses tight-binding and wave-packet calculations to theoretically explain the asymmetry via mode selection.
why_interesting: The concept of engineered, symmetry-preserving directional transport in solid-state systems is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems, offering a solid-state analogue to photonic diodes.
